summary:
MARSOL30 is a fast-paced, 2.5D survival strategy web game designed to teach children aged 7 to 12 the critical complexities of off-world life support.

Players command a four-astronaut crew stranded on Mars, racing against a 300-second timer to survive 30 Martian days (Sols). The game directly addresses the challenge by translating authentic NASA standards—such as NASA-STD-3001 human-system requirements and ECLSS closed-loop water recycling—into an intuitive arcade experience. Players sequentially build and manually operate vital base modules, manage daily consumption of power, water, oxygen, and food, shield structures from cosmic radiation using Martian soil, and execute a high-stakes endgame fuel refinement to launch back to Earth by Sol 30.

MARSOL30 is important because it bridges complex aerospace engineering and EdTech. By requiring zero installation and running instantly in any web browser with custom AI-generated visuals, it transforms static scientific data into an engaging, interactive STEM learning tool that inspires the next generation of space explorers.
details:
Project Overview: What It Does & How It Works

MARSOL30 is a fast-paced, 2.5D survival strategy web game designed to teach children aged 7 to 12 the harsh realities of off-world life support.

Players take command of a four-astronaut crew stranded on Mars and must survive for 30 Martian days (Sols)—compressed into an intense 300-second (5-minute) race against time (1 Sol = 10 seconds)—before launching safely back to Earth.

  • Active Resource Management: Players sequentially construct and manually operate six core modules: the Mars Lander (MAV), Habitation Module (Hab), Command Center, Solar Arrays, Water Recovery System (WRS), and Greenhouse. Players must actively click inside module interfaces to convert Power and Water into vital Oxygen and Food to offset constant daily crew consumption.
  • Environmental Hazards & Endgame Trade-offs: Players must continuously shield base structures using Martian regolith ("Add Soil") to block lethal cosmic radiation. From Sol 25 onwards, a strategic twist unlocks: players can dismantle non-essential structures (excluding the Hab) to refine extra rocket fuel, requiring them to fill the Lander's fuel tank to 100% before Sol 30 ends to achieve liftoff.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Accessible STEM Education: Traditional space science textbooks are static and fail to convey the urgency of closed-loop ecosystems. MARSOL30 transforms complex aerospace engineering into an intuitive, cause-and-effect simulation where players directly experience how a failure in one system triggers a domino effect across the entire base.
  • Immediate Classroom & Home Readiness: Built as a lightweight, browser-ready web application requiring zero installation, MARSOL30 can be immediately adopted by teachers, parents, and students worldwide as an interactive STEM learning tool to inspire the next generation of space explorers and systems thinkers.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

  • Bridging NASA Authenticity with Arcade Pacing: Rather than inventing arbitrary game numbers, we anchored our mechanics in real NASA engineering standards (NASA-STD-3001 and ECLSS). We incorporated actual Martian parameters—such as solar irradiance being 44% of Earth's, 98% wastewater recycling efficiency, daily astronaut consumption rates, and ~0.67 mSv/day surface radiation—and scaled them into an engaging 5-minute arcade loop.
  • Age-Appropriate UX & AI-Generated Visuals: Designing for a 7–12 age demographic required balancing scientific depth with clarity. To achieve a cohesive, immersive look, all game asset graphics and visual concepts were entirely generated using Gemini, paired with an interactive 15-page in-game tutorial, a game-speed toggle (Speed x1), and strategic mechanics like the Sol 25 dismantling system.

Tools, Software & Technologies Used

  • Game Engine & Programming: Godot Engine 4 (GDScript) for core simulation loops, UI state management, and WebGL/HTML5 export.
  • Visual Art & Assets: Custom 2.5D graphics and sprite elements entirely generated using Gemini.
  • Scientific Reference Data: NASA-STD-3001 (Space Flight Human-System Standard), NASA ECLSS (Environmental Control and Life Support System) specifications, and SwRI research on Mars.

Acknowledgments & Credits

  • Audio Assets (Sound Effects & Music): Adapted from Mindustry by Anuken, utilized under the terms of the GNU GPL v3.0 license. We sincerely thank the open-source community for providing these audio resources to enhance the player experience in MARSOL30.
